issues.legal_issue: A pre-amendment land acquisition for a company may be retrospectively validated where the acquisition was completed, the land vested in the government, and the acquisition met the requirements for a company engaged in an industry or work serving a public purpose.
material_facts: The acquisition proceedings began before the amendment took effect, and the required acquisition notification was published before then.
An award was made, the land vested in the government, and possession was delivered to the company before the amendment took effect.
The land was acquired for construction or work connected with a company engaged in manufacturing goods that benefited the public and reduced reliance on imports.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition satisfied the conditions for retrospective validation and the challenge to its validity failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1962 validated qualifying acquisitions made before July 20, 1962, notwithstanding court orders, if the acquisition was complete and the land had vested absolutely in the government under section 16 or section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and the acquisition fell within section 40(1)(aa) as amended. The Court applied the interpretation in R. L. Arora v. State of U.P. (the second Arora case) and followed Himalayan Tiles and Marbles v. Francis Victor Coutinho.

rule.if: appeal_challenging_land_acquisition and acquisition_before_amendment and land_vested_in_government and company_industry_served_public_purpose and acquired_work_served_company_public_purpose

predicates.appeal_challenging_land_acquisition: The proceeding was an appeal challenging the validity of a compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_before_amendment: The acquisition was made before the relevant amendment took effect.
predicates.land_vested_in_government: The acquisition was completed and the land vested absolutely in the government.
predicates.company_industry_served_public_purpose: The company was engaged, or was taking steps to engage, in an industry or work that served a public purpose.
predicates.acquired_work_served_company_public_purp: The building or work for which the land was acquired served the public purpose of the company's industry or work.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenging a land acquisition concerns an acquisition made before the amendment, and the land vested in the government for work serving the public purpose of the company's industry, the acquisition is retroactively valid.

issues.legal_issue: For acquisition for a company engaged in a public-purpose industry, the required public purpose is assessed by whether the building or work serves the public purpose of the company, with regard to the nature and benefits of its industry, rather than by requiring a public purpose in the general sense.
material_facts: The company manufactured sodium silicate, plaster of Paris and other goods that were widely used and had previously been imported on a large scale.
The company's production saved foreign exchange and benefited the public.
The company sought adjoining land to expand production and provide space for underground storage tanks.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition served the public purpose of the company because the proposed expansion supported an industry whose products benefited the public and saved foreign exchange.
issues.legal_principle: Section 40(1)(aa) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended, requires that the building or work serve the public purpose of the company; the words “public purpose” take their colour from the nature of the industry, its products, and the benefit they provide. The Court applied R. L. Arora v. State of U.P. (the second Arora case), approved the approach in P. Girdharan Prasad Missair v. State of Bihar and Chhotubhai Babarbhai Patel v. State of Gujarat, and also referred to the second Arora case’s treatment of production serving the general public.

predicates.land_acquisition_for_company: The land was acquired for construction or work for a company.
predicates.company_industry_benefited_public: The company's industry or work produced benefits for the public, considering its products and their economic or practical effects.
predicates.acquired_work_supported_company_industry: The building or work for which the land was acquired supported the company's industry or work.

issues.definition: When land is acquired for a company whose industry benefits the public and the proposed work supports that industry, the acquisition serves the company's public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: The restriction in section 44B of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, does not apply to acquisition proceedings commenced before the amendment took effect.
material_facts: The acquisition proceedings were commenced before the amendment took effect.
The acquisition notification, award, vesting of the land, and delivery of possession all occurred before that date.
issues.conclusion: Section 44B did not apply to these acquisition proceedings because it was prospective.
issues.legal_principle: Section 44B of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended, is prospective and does not apply to acquisition proceedings taken before July 20, 1962.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerned compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.proceeding_started_before_amendment: The acquisition proceeding began before the relevant amendment took effect.

issues.definition: A later restriction does not apply when a land acquisition proceeding began before the amendment took effect.

issues.legal_issue: Permitting acquisition for a company while not extending the same acquisition power to individuals or private companies does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The challenge alleged unequal treatment because the acquisition power was available for a company but not for an individual or a private company, even if they engaged in an industry serving a public purpose.
The acquisition power was part of a statutory scheme directed to acquisition for qualifying companies and their public-purpose work.
issues.conclusion: Section 40(1)(aa) did not violate Article 14 of the Constitution by drawing that distinction.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a distinction between companies eligible for acquisition under section 40(1)(aa) and private individuals or private companies, having regard to the object of the clause. The Court followed the ruling in R. L. Arora v. State of U.P. (the second Arora case).

predicates.challenge_to_company_acquisition_classif: The proceeding challenged the different treatment of companies and other persons in access to compulsory land acquisition.
predicates.acquisition_power_limited_to_qualifying_: The acquisition power was available for qualifying companies but not on the same basis for individuals or private companies.
predicates.classification_related_to_statutory_obje: The distinction was related to the purpose of enabling acquisition for qualifying companies and their public-purpose work.

issues.definition: When a challenged distinction limits acquisition powers to qualifying companies and is related to the purpose of that power, the classification does not violate equality.
